messages.body_plain:
Hello

=20

We counted the numbers of birds seen in an area of sea from a low flying
aircraft, flying along parallel line transects, using standard JNCC
aerial survey methods.  The raw data were processed through Distance to
estimate the total number of birds in the entire survey area.   =20
=20
We then selected a subsection of the area of search, selecting areas of
higher density.  We want to estimate the numbers of birds within the
higher density subsection. =20
=20
If we use Distance, we are deliberately shortening transects to exclude
sections of transects where no or few birds were seen, with the result
that our estimate of numbers of birds within the higher density area is
similar or sometimes greater than in the total area of search.  Eric, in
a correspondence dated 9 April, you say, "Transect length needs to
accurately reflect the amount of effort expended in the survey.  I worry
that you might adjust transect length to remove sections of transect
where effort was expended but nothing was seen.  That would badly bias
the estimated density or abundance."
=20
If distance is not a suitable method for estimating the numbers of birds
within the higher density area, do you have any suggestions for
alternative methods?
=20
Thanks in advance for your help
=20
Sue

messages.subject: Re: if Distance gives bias estimates when transects are shortened
messages.subject_clean: if Distance gives bias estimates when transects are shortened
messages.body_plain:
Sue, data-dependent post-stratification of this type is prone to bias.
This isn't something specific to Distance.  However, if you're in the
situation that there really aren't any birds in the areas where none
were detected, and almost all the birds are within the region you've
identified from the data, bias is likely to be small.  Note though that
even if bias in quantifying what was there at the time of the survey is
small, many of those birds might be outside that small area next day -
or even later the same day.

Depending on how clustered the distribution is, you might want to
consider using Distance to fit density surface models - and you can
estimate numbers in any sub-area of interest by integrating under the
parts of that surface corresponding to the sub-area.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Replacement of clusters by individuals
messages.subject_clean: Replacement of clusters by individuals
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Is there a way to deal with animals that form loose aggregations rather than
defined groups (clusters). The data that was collected was in the form of
clusters, where most individuals were detected as single objects, but once
in while two to six. Antelopes such as Springbok in Southern Africa do form
herds, but when food is abundant, the herds can spread over miles, which
makes it difficult to define a herd. Then again, occasionally they do form
i.e. bachelor herds.
Can the data collected as clusters be replaced by individuals. Does this
greatly violate the assumptions of distance? When data is collected, should
all animals be collected as single objects, even though they do sometimes
occur in smaller groups (violation of independence)? It might also be that
the Springbok is a difficult case. Would another option be to do an analysis
seperately for clusters and non-clusters and then add the estimates to
obtain a global estimate?

thanks for any suggestions on the topic: loose aggregations.

Johanna.

messages.subject: Re: Replacement of clusters by individuals
messages.subject_clean: Replacement of clusters by individuals
messages.body_plain:
Johanna, the methods are very robust to failures of the independence
assumption, which means that, in your case, you would be better to
analyse the data ignoring clusters.  If there are 6 animals in a group,
record 6 individual distances.  This can cause the goodness-of-fit test
statistics to give spurious significant results, but otherwise causes
few problems.  You can also record which animals were part of the same
herd, which allows you to analyse the data either way for example, to
assess whether it makes any practical difference.  You then need to find
a mean distance from the line of a group - for a group that has
individuals both sides of the line, you need to be careful to record
distances on one side as negative, before taking the mean distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

This mail is to find out suggestions for a possible technique suitable
for the population estimation of Nilgiri tahr (Hemitragus hylocrius
Ogilby), a mountain goat in the Eravikulam National Park. The Park  is
situated in the High Ranges of the Western Ghats in India. It covers
an area of about 97 sq km and is of undulating terrain comprising a
high rolling plateau with a base elevation of about 2000 m. Most of
the peaks rise 100-300 m above this plateau. The horizontally and
vertically rounded cliffs are the characteristic features of the Park.
 The terrain  is covered primarily with the grasslands and small
patches of forest in gullies and hollows.=A0 Shrub lands are found along
the bases of cliffs and intersperse in rocky areas.

Nilgiri tahr lives in herds and sensitive to the presence of human.
The preferred habitats of the tahr are rocky outcrops set amongst
grass hills and cliffs bordering grasslands to escape from predators.

The tahr population in the Park is usually estimated by the Park
Mangers using bounded count technique (Regier and Robson,1966). Twelve
blocks based on the home range, were taken as the basic units for the
population estimation.  Although bounded count  is rarely used for
terrestrial animal species, application of this method several times
in the past reveals that it does provide the reasonable estimates of
the tahr population.

However, there are suggestions that other techniques should be tried
because  the bounded count does not involve probability of animal
detection.

Placing line transects is very difficult in the highly undulating
terrain. Therefore, the line transect sampling is not suitable.

 Anyone would like to suggest a technique which we can attempt to
estimate the population of this endangered species?.

Reference:

Regier, H.A. and D.S. Robson (1966). Estimating population numbers and
=A0 mortality=A0=A0 rates.=A0 In: S.D. Gerking (ed.). The biological basis =
of
fresh water fish production.=A0 Blackwell Scientific Publication,
Oxford, U.K.

M.Sivaram
Scientist
Kerala Forest Research Institute
Peechi - 680653
Kerala State
India

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am looking at comparing a number of methods used to estimate kangaroo n=
umbers, which includes walked line transect surveys, and driven line tran=
sect surveys from tracks. I am aware of issues with track-based surveys, =
but due to the advantages relating to access and speed, I really want to =
get track-based surveys working. I am working in a 400ha fenced reserve, =
with a high density population of kangaroos of known number, in a woodlan=
d habitat. The first survey was conducted over 16 transects (approx 600m =
each), a second survey was also done using same tracks. This has not been=
 analyzed yet . Kangaroos were recorded from 75 points, with over 270 ani=
mals seen.  The results of analysis in distance produced population estim=
ates of around half the known number. Underestimation maybe expected , bu=
t I believe some of this underestimate is due to issues with my design an=
d analysis. I have a number of questions relating to overlapping tracks, =
double counting, and low detection rate near line.=20
I have attached a map of the tracks used in survey with email. As you can=
 see some tracks/lines  are very close, resulting in significant overlap =
of effective strip widths between lines. I understand overlapping transec=
ts are not a problem, but perhaps the number of tracks overlapping in thi=
s case is too high, thus explaining part of the underestimate.=20
Another issue is double counting animals. I understand an animal should o=
nly be counted once, regardless of whether they can be seen from multiple=
 transects. Further, I assume perpendicular distance of animal should be =
recorded from the transect they were first seen, regardless of animal act=
ually being closer to a different track. Because I number of tracks are c=
lose, this situation often occurred, with many tracks recording zero anim=
als despite animals being clearly visible from tracks. I figure I should =
double count animals seen from different lines, as the length of two line=
s recording similar animals is leading to underestimation of population. =
Perhaps this is another reason to cut tracks, which are overlapping each =
other.
The final issue encountered comes from the detection curve. I have attach=
ed a graph form Distance. Such low detection probabilities near the line =
may have resulted from animals moving away from track before they were re=
corded, or maybe because animals generally avoid tracks. This is possible=
, although vegetation near road appears as grazed as vegetation further f=
rom road. And animals were generally recorded before they moved, indicati=
ng low response to observer approach.  How would others deal with this ki=
nd of detection curve? I tried cutting all detections within 30m of track=
 as part of truncation, which did improve the model fit, but is this the =
correct approach? I find this a difficult problem to solve.

Appreciate any feedback in trying to improve the population estimates giv=
en from my survey design.

Regards

g(0)<1, but you still need to fight your battle about representativeness =

an animal once that is visible from more than one line.  It is generally =

poor practice to have such overlapping - in part because animals may=20
move in response to the observer, giving a biased sample when you survey =

the next line.  However, if you do overlap lines, you must record any=20
animals seen from any line, whether or not an animal has been detected=20
from a different line.

Steve Buckland

in your decay rates, you are using the 'retrospective' method of

coefficients.

Meredith of WCS Malaysia has put together on estimating decay rates
using the retrospective method

Sacha:

I wish to give one more suggestion for the analysis of data relating
to decay rate. I had an opportunity to analyze the data of dung decay
experiments conducted following Laing et al. (2003) in connection with
the population estimation of elephants.  However, it was observed from
the detailed analysis that the data collected were not found to follow
the logistic regression model. So, we had to resort to alternative
statistical technique for analysis. We used Kaplan-Meier survivorship
function (Hosmer and  Lemeshow 1999) for estimating average survival
time of the dung piles (referred to as time to decay). The
Kaplan-Meier survival analysis is free of models (non-parametric).
Log-rank test (non-parametric) was used for comparing two or more
survival curves across different habitats. I hope this hint might help
in the analysis of your data.

REFERENCES:
1)	LAING, S.E., BUCKLAND, S.T., BURNS, R.W., LAMBIE, D.  & AMPHLETT,
A. (2003): Dung and nest surveys: estimating decay rates. Journal of
Applied Ecology, 40: 1102-111.
2)	HOSMER, DAVID W.  & STANLEY LEMESHOW (1999): Applied Survival
Analysis: regression modeling of time to event data. A
Wiley-Interscience Publication, John Wiley & Sons, New York.

> > Hello all, a couple of questions, kind of new so I apoligize if these questions are obvious. I'm studying a species of grouse and am concerned that some animals move prior to detection and do not flush at all. Histograms of the distances recorded do not highlight evasive movements but perhaps this is because they are holding into the cover or moving beyond the flushing distance. Is there any way to account for this and might this bias my results to the point where the distance technique fails on this particular species??
Yes, if a significant proportion of your birds do this, then the method
will fail - and there is no guarantee that there will be evidence of
this behaviour in the histograms of data.  This can be a problem for
gamebirds.  It's possible that working a trained dog may reduce the
problem - but it takes a while to train the dog!  Another possibility is
if you could estimate the proportion of birds that do this, e.g. by
radio-tagging a few birds, then you could add a correction as a
'multiplier'.  Or you could use radio-tagged birds for trials - send an
observer past a bird with known location and note whether the observer
records it.  You can estimate a detection function given enough trials
of this type, using say logistic regression.  No easy solution I'm afraid.
> >
> >
> > Beyond the issues above, we also have a pretty low encounter rate; we flush about 20 birds per sample season. Am I wrong to want to pool data across years to better model the detection process then use that global detection function to estimate abundance annually? Is this too simplistic or does there need to be statistical justification to pool across years to develop a detection function? My thought is that because survey timing is the same from year to year, w/ the same observers on the same transects, the detection process should be consistent across years. Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated. DAVE
> >
That is easier - yes, you can pool data if you believe the detection
function will be constant.  Probably better to test this though, for
example by using the mcds engine of Distance, and entering year as a
factor-type covariate.  That allows you to test whether you can assume
the same detection function across years - and provides a means of
estimating different detection functions for each year from the pooled
data, to avoid the small sample size problem.

Dear member's list,

I'm using for the first time the Distance software and I have some questions
about comparing my results from each area (3) First, it was decide to treat
the different areas seperately because the main objective of this study is
to see the diferenciation of occupancy among two species in those areas
(guanacos,huemules) also the visibility aren't the same due to different
vegetation  and also because a post-stratification by cluster size seems
accurate in the case of the guanacos. I'm now trying to establish if my
datas are distributed normally in each areas  and then do a statistic
analysis (ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis) to see if there's a significant
difference among the areas for each specie. To see if the distribution of my
datas is normal, I was thinking to use the density (D= N/2wL) for each
transect and then compare them...is it a better way to do it?

foxes in the areas. Since we don't have the decay rate and the number of
faeces produced daily by foxes, I think the only information I can use is
the index of faeces by kilometer of transect. I don't think I can use
Distance's software since we don't have the perpendicular Distance either
(the faeces were on the line). Is there an other option? And if not, can we
compare this index among the transects to see if the datas are distributed
normally?(like the datas collected for the guanacos and huemules)

Many thanks,

Julie Langevin
Student in international ecology of the University of Sherbrooke, Canada
